newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK's pro-democracy groups stage boisterous rallies.
newsitem.headline: HK's pro-democracy groups stage boisterous rallies.

text.p: Pro-democracy activists poured into Hong Kong's streets in the early hours of Tuesday, staging boisterous rallies and vowing to fight for civil liberties now that Communist China has taken over the territory.
"The message is that we want democracy and we want it now," said pro-democracy leader Emily Lau at a rally in Statue Square in central Hong Kong where at least 1,000 people had gathered.
She had just led hundreds of people carrying a giant yellow ribbon in a walk around the central legislature building.
"The yellow ribbon is our wish that democracy returns," said Lee Cheuk-yan, another pro-democracy leader.
Beijing dissolved the elected legislature after taking over the British colony at midnight on Monday and was set to swear in its own hand-picked assembly within hours.
Members of Hong Kong's Democratic Party refused to join the pro-Beijing assembly and have launched a protest campaign.

In the nearby Wan Chai district, the April 5 action group pushed and shoved with police. Protesters carried aloft a large paper model of a Chinese army tank to symbolise the crushing of mass student-led demonstrations centred on Tiananmen Square in Beijing on June 4, 1989.
A dozen April 5 protesters carried banners with slogans sure to draw Beijing's ire, including "Down with (Premier) Li Peng" and "Remember the June 4 Slaughter".

The Democratic Party vowed to enter the legislature building in the early hours of Tuesday to stage a protest on the balcony while the pro-Beijing assembly was sworn in at the nearby Convention Centre.
Protesters in Statue Square chanted "Sovereignty belongs to the people" and "Down with (Beijing's) provisional legislature".
Demonstrators in the crowd expressed anger at curbs which Hong Kong's new chief executive Tung Chee-hwa imposed on political reforms adopted in the twilight of British rule.

"Democracy came too late in Hong Kong and now it's getting worse. Hong Kong people aren't very political but they care about democracy and they're worried about life under the Communists," said one of the leaders of the Pioneer Group.
Many demonstrators in the square said they would march to Tung's office after China formally took over Hong Kong and then to the convention centre where the handover was held.
"Today is the first day under new sovereignty. Today is going to be the first major battle for democracy. We will win in the end," said pro-democracy leader Szeto Wah.
Legislator Lee Wing Tat told the crowd: "We all know that the way to democracy is long and difficult. We do not see smooth sailing ahead."
